<reason>A high-quality, genuinely contested debate. A (CON) built a real case: treatment is opt-in and can't scale in five years, naloxone needs a witness and can't be self-administered, and the 2024 decline coincided with record enforcement. A prosecuted the "chain of voluntary steps" framing effectively to the end. But the debate turned on mechanism for the supply-side path. A's case ran through price (A1.7: "higher prices... suppress initiation"; A2.6: higher prices "shrink how much current users can buy"). B's Q1 forced the issue, and A's R2 conceded price cannot transmit for cheap synthetic fentanyl — a retreat B's closing correctly identified as load-bearing: without price, the initiation-suppression and pool-shrinkage channels collapse, leaving tonnage and indictments (activity, not scarcity). B's unfalsifiability charge (rise = "restructuring," fall = pressure "caught up") stuck, since A counted both the post-2019 rise and 2024 fall as enforcement success. Meanwhile B answered A's discontinuity challenge directly with a plausible step change (OTC naloxone switch, settlement-funded surge, nonlinear saturation threshold, east-to-west gradient), and A's rebuttal addressed only the settlement money. B's surviving route — medication halves mortality even inside a saturated supply, which both sides' accounts imply persists through 2030 — was the cleaner five-year path. Both sides followed Q/A format and stayed epistemically disciplined; A remained competitive throughout on coverage and consent.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 → A's R2 concession that fentanyl pressure "cannot transmit through price" → B's closing showing this guts A's initiation-suppression and pool-shrinkage mechanisms, capped by the unfalsifiability tag ("a theory that fits every outcome predicts none"). This sequence dismantled CON's primary causal pathway; A's closing reframe ("a concession about their test, not our mechanism") asserted rather than repaired.</best_rebuttal>
